name: Rice Blast
overview: The most destructive fungal disease of rice worldwide. It attacks leaves, nodes, neck and panicle, and can cause total loss in a susceptible variety under favourable weather.
image_cues: Photograph a single affected leaf flat and in even light. Blast lesions are spindle or diamond shaped with a grey-white centre and a dark brown margin.
symptoms: Spindle (diamond) shaped spots on leaves with grey-white centres and brown margins
Lesions enlarge and merge, killing the whole leaf (leaf blast)
Black discolouration at the node (node blast) which snaps the stem
Neck blast: brown-black rot at the panicle base causing the panicle to hang and chaffy grains
Severe cases produce a burnt or scorched appearance across the field
favourable: High humidity (above 90%) with leaf wetness
Temperature 24–28 °C with intermittent rain and cloudy days
Excess nitrogen fertiliser making leaf blades lush and soft
Continuous fog or dew over several days
spread: Airborne spores spread over long distances. Survives in infected seed and crop residue. Wind and rain splash move spores between fields.

cultural: Use blast-resistant varieties recommended for your region.
Split nitrogen into 3 doses and avoid excess or late nitrogen.
Maintain balanced silicon and potassium nutrition to toughen leaf blades.
Avoid dense planting; provide good air movement.
Burn or incorporate infected residue after harvest.
organic: Pseudomonas fluorescens or Bacillus subtilis seed treatment and foliar spray.
Neem oil or Trichoderma-based sprays reduce spread when applied early.
Silicon supplementation (rice husk ash) is a cheap preventive measure.
chemical: Seed treatment with carbendazim or tricyclazole before sowing.
Foliar spray of tricyclazole 75% WP (0.6 g/L) or isoprothiolane at boot leaf stage.
Repeat spray at 50% heading if neck blast pressure is high.
Rotate fungicide groups to avoid resistance.

prevention: Treat seed with hot water (52–54 °C for 10 minutes) or a fungicide.
Destroy stubble and weeds that host the fungus.
Balance nitrogen with potassium and silicon.

name: Bacterial Leaf Blight
overview: A serious bacterial disease that typically appears at tillering and can cause up to 50% yield loss. It is especially damaging when heavy rain or flooding follows fertiliser application.
image_cues: Look for yellowish-white stripes running along the leaf margins from the tip downwards. Early morning you may see milky bacterial ooze on the leaf.
symptoms: Water-soaked to yellowish stripes starting at the leaf tip or margin
Lesions turn straw white or pale yellow and extend along the veins
Leaves roll, dry and turn greyish white (kresek) in severe early infection
Milky or yellowish bacterial ooze appears on cut ends in the morning
Wilting of seedlings within weeks of transplanting in the kresek form
favourable: Heavy rain, strong winds and flooding
High humidity and temperature around 25–30 °C
Excess nitrogen with low soil potassium
Standing water after storms
spread: Bacteria survive in seed, stubble and irrigation water. Enter through leaf wounds and hydathodes. Wind-driven rain and flood water spread infection rapidly.

cultural: Grow resistant varieties and avoid very susceptible ones after a wet forecast.
Drain the field and stop nitrogen when symptoms appear.
Avoid clipping seedling tips at transplanting, which creates entry wounds.
Do not flood the field immediately after applying urea.
organic: Pseudomonas fluorescens seed treatment and spray.
Balanced potassium and calcium nutrition reduces susceptibility.
Copper-based sprays (Bordeaux mixture 1%) reduce spread.
chemical: Streptocycline seed soak (0.025%) followed by two sprays at 10-day intervals.
Copper oxychloride 2.5 g/L with streptocycline 0.15 g/L at early symptom stage.
There is no direct cure; these sprays only slow the epidemic.

prevention: Use certified disease-free seed.
Avoid excess nitrogen and keep potassium adequate.
Drain fields after heavy rain to reduce water spread.

name: Rice Brown Spot (Helminthosporium)
overview: A common disease of nutritionally stressed or drought-affected rice. It was the primary cause of the historic Bengal famine and remains important on marginal soils.
image_cues: Oval brown spots with a lighter centre and a yellow halo scattered evenly over the leaf.
symptoms: Small oval to circular brown spots with a grey or light centre
Spots have a distinct yellow halo and are evenly scattered
Severe infection coalesces and turns leaves brown
favourable: Nutrient deficient or drought-stressed soil
High humidity with warm temperature around 25–30 °C
Poorly drained or lateritic soils low in silicon and potassium
spread: Seed-borne and air-borne. Spreads through rain splash and spores in the air.

cultural: Correct soil fertility, especially nitrogen, potassium and silicon.
Avoid water stress; maintain proper irrigation.
Use certified treated seed.
organic: Trichoderma seed treatment.
Silicon supplementation through rice husk ash.
Improved organic matter to boost general plant vigour.
chemical: Seed treatment with carbendazim or mancozeb.
Foliar spray of mancozeb 2 g/L or propiconazole 1 ml/L at the boot stage if severe.

prevention: Keep the crop well nourished and free from drought stress.
Use healthy seed and improve soil organic matter.

name: Rice Sheath Blight
overview: A soil-borne disease that attacks the leaf sheath near the water line, causing lodging and unfilled grains in dense, high-nitrogen crops.
image_cues: Photograph the lower stem and sheath. Look for greenish-grey oval lesions with a distinct brown border, often with a banded pattern.
symptoms: Oval greenish-grey lesions on the sheath near the water line
Lesions have a brown margin and often show a banded pattern
Sheath rots, the plant lodges, and panicles fail to fill
Webby white mycelium and small brown sclerotia visible in severe cases
favourable: Dense planting with high humidity
High nitrogen levels
Continuous flooding and warm temperature 28–32 °C
spread: Survives as sclerotia in soil and stubble. Spreads through flood water and contact between plants.

cultural: Reduce plant density and split nitrogen applications.
Adopt AWD instead of continuous flooding.
Deep plough to bury sclerotia.
organic: Trichoderma viride soil application.
Pseudomonas fluorescens foliar spray.
chemical: Hexaconazole 2 ml/L or validamycin 2.5 ml/L sprayed at the sheath.
Propiconazole plus a sticker to reach the lower sheath.

prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen and very dense stands.
Rotate with a non-host crop such as pulses.

name: Wheat Leaf Rust (Brown Rust)
overview: The most widely distributed wheat rust. Orange-brown pustules on the leaves reduce photosynthesis and can cut yield by 20–40% in an early epidemic.
image_cues: Sharp photo of the upper leaf surface showing many small round orange-brown pustules scattered randomly, not in neat lines.
symptoms: Round to oval orange-brown pustules scattered randomly on the leaf blade
Pustules erupt through the leaf surface and rub off as orange powder
Leaves yellow and dry from the tip as the infection advances
favourable: Cool to warm temperature 15–22 °C
High humidity with dew or intermittent rain
Late sowing and a long vegetative period
spread: Airborne spores travel hundreds of kilometres. The disease builds up fastest in warm, humid February–March weather.

cultural: Grow rust-resistant varieties suited to your region.
Sow on time to avoid a late, prolonged rust season.
Avoid excess nitrogen which makes leaves more susceptible.
organic: Sulphur dust or sulphur-based sprays give partial control.
Neem-based formulations reduce spore germination but are weak alone.
chemical: Propiconazole 25% EC 1 ml/L spray at first sign of pustules.
Tebuconazole 1 ml/L or a triazole plus strobilurin mix for a strong protective effect.
Spray in the morning with a high water volume (about 400 L/ha) for good coverage.

prevention: Monitor fields weekly from January and act on the very first pustules.
Use resistant varieties and destroy volunteer wheat plants that carry the fungus.

name: Wheat Stripe Rust (Yellow Rust)
overview: A devastating cool-weather rust that can destroy a crop within weeks if left unchecked. It is a notifiable disease in several countries.
image_cues: Photograph the leaf surface. Yellow-orange pustules form in neat parallel lines (stripes) between the veins.
symptoms: Bright yellow to orange pustules arranged in stripes between the leaf veins
Leaves split and shred, turning pale and dying early
Pustules also appear on the sheath, glumes and awns
favourable: Cool temperature 8–18 °C with high humidity and dew
Cloudy weather during the vegetative stage
Late sowing and a susceptible variety
spread: Wind-blown spores can travel very long distances and cause sudden regional epidemics.

cultural: Sow resistant varieties and avoid highly susceptible ones in cool, wet valleys.
Destroy volunteer wheat that bridges the season.
Sow on time to escape the cool epidemic window.
organic: Sulphur sprays have limited effect at high disease pressure.
Focus on resistant varieties rather than organic control.
chemical: Propiconazole 1 ml/L or tebuconazole 1 ml/L immediately at the first pustules.
Repeat after 15 days if the weather stays cool and humid.
Use a mix of Triazole + Strobilurin for a longer protective period.

prevention: Scout relentlessly in cool, humid periods and spray at first sight.
Report unusual outbreaks to your local agriculture office — it spreads regionally.

name: Wheat Powdery Mildew
overview: A white powdery growth on leaves and stems of densely sown, heavily fertilised wheat. It reduces tillering and grain filling.
image_cues: White to grey powdery patches on the upper leaf surface and stem, easy to rub off with a finger.
symptoms: White to grey powdery patches on leaves, sheaths and stems
The powder can be wiped off, revealing yellow or brown leaf tissue below
Leaves turn yellow and dry prematurely in severe attacks
favourable: Temperature 15–22 °C with high humidity and cloudy weather
Dense sowing and lush growth from excess nitrogen
Poor air movement in sheltered fields
spread: Airborne conidia spread during the growing season; the fungus also survives on crop residue.

cultural: Reduce sowing density and avoid excess nitrogen.
Grow resistant varieties.
Ensure good air circulation and adequate potassium.
organic: Potassium bicarbonate or milk spray (1:9) gives partial control.
Sulphur-based sprays work well against powdery mildew specifically.
chemical: Sulphur 80% WP 2 g/L or wettable sulphur spray at early stages.
Propiconazole 1 ml/L or a strobilurin mix if the disease is severe.
Apply with good coverage of the upper leaf surface.

prevention: Balance nitrogen and potassium in the fertiliser schedule.
Use clean seed and avoid very dense stands.

name: Wheat Karnal Bunt
overview: A seed- and soil-borne smut that partially converts grains into a black powdery mass with a fishy smell. Even a small incidence causes market rejection because of quarantine restrictions.
image_cues: Photograph split infected grains — the kernel is partly replaced with black powder. Leaf symptoms are absent, so ear and grain photos matter most.
symptoms: Partially bunted grains with a black powdery mass and a fishy smell
Only part of the grain is affected, unlike loose smut
Symptoms visible only at maturity when the earhead opens
favourable: Cool, wet weather with high humidity during ear emergence
Irrigation during flowering with cloudy conditions
Infected seed or soil-borne spores
spread: Spores survive in soil and on seed. Wind and rain splash carry spores to the flowering spike.

cultural: Use certified disease-free seed.
Avoid irrigation during ear emergence and flowering.
Rotate with a non-host crop for at least one season.
organic: Solarisation of soil and removal of infected earheads.
Trichoderma soil application offers some suppression.
chemical: Seed treatment with carboxin or tebuconazole formulation.
Propiconazole spray at ear emergence reduces infection.
Deep summer ploughing to bury spores.

prevention: Never save seed from an infected field.
Time irrigation to avoid flowering-stage wetness.

name: Northern Corn Leaf Blight
overview: Large cigar-shaped grey-green lesions on maize leaves that destroy leaf area and can cause 30–50% yield loss in humid weather.
image_cues: Photograph a leaf showing long, cigar or boat-shaped grey-green to tan lesions with smooth rounded ends.
symptoms: Long, cigar or boat-shaped grey-green lesions, 3–15 cm long
Lesions turn tan or brown with dark spore masses in the centre
Heavy infection dries the leaves from the lower canopy upwards
favourable: Temperature 18–27 °C with high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness
Cloudy, rainy weather for several days
Continuous maize cropping and surface residue
spread: Airborne spores plus residue-borne inoculum. Wind and rain spread the disease quickly within a field.

cultural: Grow resistant hybrids — the cheapest and most effective control.
Rotate with a non-host crop and incorporate residue after harvest.
Avoid overhead irrigation in the evening.
organic: Trichoderma and Pseudomonas sprays reduce inoculum.
Neem oil spray limits spread when applied early.
chemical: Mancozeb 2.5 g/L or chlorothalonil 2 g/L at first lesions.
Propiconazole 1 ml/L for a stronger curative effect.
Repeat after 12–15 days if the weather stays humid.

prevention: Rotate maize with soybean, groundnut or another legume.
Use resistant hybrids in high-humidity regions.

name: Gray Leaf Spot (Maize)
overview: Rectangular grey-brown lesions that run parallel to the veins. It is a residue-borne disease that builds up in continuous no-till maize.
image_cues: Photograph the leaf. Lesions are narrow, rectangular and strictly limited by the veins, giving a streaky grey-brown look.
symptoms: Narrow rectangular lesions bounded by leaf veins
Lesions are tan to grey-brown, often with a faint yellow halo
Severe infection causes the whole leaf to blight and die
favourable: Warm humid weather 25–30 °C with extended leaf wetness
Continuous no-till maize with surface residue
High humidity and dew periods over 12 hours
spread: Spores from crop residue are splashed and blown onto new leaves.

cultural: Rotate away from maize for one season and bury residue.
Use tolerant hybrids.
Avoid late planting in a humid season.
organic: Residue management is the key organic measure.
Bio-fungicide sprays give only partial control.
chemical: Azoxystrobin plus propiconazole at first symptoms.
Mancozeb 2.5 g/L for protective cover.

prevention: Tillage or residue removal reduces inoculum strongly.
Use a maize–legume rotation.

name: Downy Mildew
overview: A systemic disease that produces yellowing and a white downy growth on the underside of leaves. Infected plants are stunted and often produce no grain.
image_cues: Photograph both leaf surfaces. The upper side shows pale yellow streaks and the underside has a white to grey downy fuzz in the morning.
symptoms: Pale yellow streaks or patches on the upper leaf surface
White to grey downy (fuzzy) growth on the underside of the leaf
Chlorotic leaves may shred into ribbons
Stunted plants with excessive tillering (green ear) and no grain
favourable: High humidity, fog and temperature 20–25 °C
Waterlogged or low-lying fields
Continuous cropping of a susceptible hybrid
spread: Soil-borne and seed-borne, with airborne spores in humid weather. Rain splash and wind move the disease.

cultural: Grow resistant hybrids.
Remove and destroy infected plants as soon as they appear.
Improve drainage and avoid low-lying waterlogged plots.
Rotate with a non-host crop.
organic: Seed treatment with Trichoderma or Pseudomonas.
Rogue out infected plants promptly.
chemical: Seed treatment with metalaxyl (Apron) at 2 g/kg seed.
Metalaxyl + mancozeb foliar spray at early symptoms.
Foliar phosphonate sprays reduce systemic spread.

prevention: Metalaxyl seed treatment is the single most effective preventive step.
Use resistant hybrids and ensure good drainage.

name: Pearl Millet Downy Mildew
overview: The most damaging disease of pearl millet, capable of wiping out a crop. It causes green ear and stunting in systemic infections.
image_cues: Look for yellowing leaves with a white downy underside growth and the distinctive green-ear symptom where the earhead becomes a leafy mass.
symptoms: Yellow to pale green streaks on leaves
White downy sporulation on the leaf underside in humid mornings
Green ear: the earhead is transformed into leafy structures
Severely stunted, tillering plants with poor or no grain
favourable: High humidity with cool nights and warm days
Rainy periods during the seedling stage
Continuous bajra cropping
spread: Soil-borne oospores and airborne sporangia. Infected seed also carries the fungus.

cultural: Plant resistant hybrids — essential in endemic areas.
Rogue out green ear plants and destroy them.
Rotate with a non-host crop for at least one season.
organic: Trichoderma seed treatment.
Rogueing infected plants early is the main organic route.
chemical: Metalaxyl seed treatment at 2 g/kg seed.
Metalaxyl + mancozeb spray if rain continues in the seedling stage.

prevention: Always treat seed with metalaxyl in downy mildew prone areas.
Remove volunteer and green-ear plants to cut soil inoculum.

name: Cotton Fusarium Wilt
overview: A soil-borne vascular wilt that causes sudden wilting and death. Once established in a field, it persists for many years.
image_cues: Photograph a wilting plant and a cut stem. Look for brown discolouration of the internal woody ring.
symptoms: Sudden wilting of the plant, often on one side first
Yellowing and drying of leaves from the lower part upwards
Brown discolouration in the internal stem tissue when cut
Root and collar rot with a dry, dark lesion
favourable: Soil temperature 25–30 °C with moderate soil moisture
Nematode infestation that opens entry points
Continuous cotton cropping and acidic soil
spread: Survives in soil and seed for many years. Spreads by movement of soil, water and farm machinery.

cultural: Use wilt-resistant varieties or rootstocks.
Rotate with a non-host crop such as a cereal for 2–3 years.
Improve drainage and raise soil pH with lime if acidic.
Remove and destroy affected plants with their roots.
organic: Trichoderma viride seed and soil application is a proven control.
Neem cake or castor cake soil application reduces the pathogen.
Solarise the soil with plastic sheets before planting.
chemical: Seed treatment with carbendazim or thiram.
Drench the collar region with carbendazim 1 g/L at the first wilt symptoms.
Fungicide drenching gives limited results on established infections.

prevention: Include a cereal rotation to reduce soil inoculum.
Use resistant varieties and certified seed.

name: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCuD)
pathogen: Cotton leaf curl virus (Begomovirus), transmitted by whitefly
overview: A whitefly-transmitted virus that stunts plants, curls leaves and drastically reduces boll formation. There is no chemical cure.
image_cues: Photograph the upper leaves showing upward curling, vein thickening, and cup-shaped leaf-like enations on the underside.
symptoms: Upward or downward curling of leaves with thickened veins
Small leaf-like outgrowths (enations) on the underside of leaves
Severely stunted plants with reduced boll formation
Dark green, leathery leaves and poor flowering
favourable: High whitefly populations in warm dry weather
Continuous cotton cropping in the same area
Presence of alternate weed hosts near the field
spread: Spread only by whitefly. Virus reservoirs include other cotton and weed hosts.

cultural: Grow CLCuD-resistant varieties.
Remove and destroy infected plants early.
Control weeds that host whitefly around the field.
Avoid late planting which coincides with peak whitefly.
organic: Yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce whitefly.
Neem oil spray reduces whitefly numbers.
Conservation of natural predators such as ladybird beetles.
chemical: Control the whitefly vector with imidacloprid 0.3 ml/L or diafenthiuron.
Spray dinotefuran or flonicamid in rotation to avoid resistance.
There is no cure for the virus itself — vector control is the only strategy.

prevention: Use resistant varieties and manage whitefly from the seedling stage.
Rogue out infected plants as soon as symptoms appear.

name: Cotton Bacterial Blight
overview: Angular water-soaked leaf spots that turn brown, plus boll rot. It is favoured by warm, wet weather and spreads through seed and rain splash.
image_cues: Photograph the leaf. Look for angular, vein-limited water-soaked spots that turn brown with a red-brown border.
symptoms: Angular water-soaked leaf spots limited by veins
Spots darken to brown with a reddish margin
Boll lesions that become round, dark and sunken
Black arm: a dark elongate lesion on the stem
favourable: Warm, wet weather with rain splash
Infected seed
High humidity for prolonged periods
spread: Seed-borne and spread by rain splash, wind and irrigation water.

cultural: Use acid-delinted and certified seed.
Rotate with a non-host crop.
Avoid excessive irrigation and working in wet fields.
organic: Bordeaux mixture 1% spray is a classic effective control.
Copper-based preparations reduce spread.
chemical: Seed treatment with streptocycline and carbendazim.
Streptocycline 0.15 g/L + copper oxychloride 2.5 g/L spray at symptom onset.

prevention: Buy acid-delinted certified seed and treat it before sowing.
Avoid overhead irrigation during humid spells.

name: Sugarcane Red Rot
overview: The most feared disease of sugarcane. It causes internal reddening with white cross bands and a sour alcoholic smell, and can destroy a crop within a season.
image_cues: Photograph a split cane. Look for reddish discolouration of the internal tissue crossed by white transverse bands.
symptoms: Third and fourth leaves turn yellow and dry from the margins
Split cane shows red internal discolouration with white cross bands
Sour, alcoholic smell from the affected cane
Stalk shrinks, becomes light and hollow, and the plant dries up
favourable: High humidity and temperature 25–30 °C with rain
Waterlogged soils
Susceptible varieties grown continuously
spread: Spread mainly by infected setts, and by soil, water and wind during the monsoon.

cultural: Use disease-free setts from a certified nursery.
Follow a 3-tier seed nursery programme.
Rogue out affected clumps with the surrounding soil and burn them.
Avoid ratooning a diseased crop.
organic: Trichoderma application in the furrow.
Hot water treatment of setts at 50 °C for 2 hours.
Avoid waterlogging through proper drainage.
chemical: Sett treatment in carbendazim 1 g/L for 15 minutes before planting.
Drench affected pockets with carbendazim and cover with fresh soil.
Fungicide treatment of seed cane is standard practice.

prevention: Never plant setts from a diseased field.
Use resistant varieties and rotate with rice or a pulse.

name: Sugarcane Smut (Whip Smut)
overview: A black whip-like structure emerges from the growing point of the cane. Affected stalks become thin and grassy and produce no recoverable sugar.
image_cues: Unmistakable: a long silvery-grey to black whip emerging from the top of the cane.
symptoms: Long whip-like black structure emerging from the growing point
Thin, grass-like tillers with narrow leaves
Affected stalks are usually thinner and taller than healthy ones
favourable: Hot dry weather followed by rain
Continuous cropping with susceptible varieties
Drought stress
spread: Airborne spores and infected setts. Spores survive in soil for months.

cultural: Use resistant varieties and disease-free setts.
Rogue out whips before they burst and release spores.
Avoid planting ratoon from an affected crop.
organic: Hot water treatment of setts at 52 °C for 30 minutes.
Trichoderma applications in the furrow.
chemical: Sett treatment with carbendazim 1 g/L for 15 minutes.
No effective field cure once the whip has formed.

prevention: Hot water or fungicide sett treatment is essential before planting.
Remove whips early and burn them.

name: Sugarcane Grassy Shoot
overview: A phytoplasma disease that turns canes into a cluster of thin, pale grassy tillers with no economic yield.
image_cues: Photograph a clump showing many thin, pale yellowish tillers crowding from the base like grass.
symptoms: Numerous thin, pale yellow to white tillers emerging from the base
Leaves become small, narrow and pale
Stunted growth with no millable cane
Prolific profuse tillering giving a grass-like tuft
favourable: Use of infected setts
Presence of the leafhopper vector
Continuous cropping
spread: Mainly through infected setts; also by leafhopper vectors.

cultural: Uproot and destroy affected clumps completely.
Use disease-free seed from a certified nursery.
Avoid ratooning affected fields.
organic: Hot water treatment of setts at 50 °C for 2 hours.
Remove alternate weed hosts around the field.
chemical: Control the leafhopper vector with a recommended insecticide.
No direct chemical cure is available.

prevention: Strictly use heat-treated, disease-free planting material.
Rogue out affected clumps early.

name: Groundnut Tikka (Leaf Spot)
overview: The most important groundnut disease. Heavy leaf spotting causes extensive defoliation and can halve the yield when it starts before flowering.
image_cues: Photograph the leaf. Early spots are dark brown with a yellow halo; late spots are black on the underside.
symptoms: Early leaf spot: dark brown circular spots with a yellow halo
Late leaf spot: blackish brown spots, mostly noticed on the leaf underside
Heavy spotting leads to premature leaf drop and a bare crop
Spots also appear on the petiole and stem
favourable: High humidity and temperature 25–30 °C with frequent rain or dew
Continuous groundnut cropping
Dense canopy that stays wet
spread: Airborne spores from crop residue are splashed and wind-blown to new leaves.

cultural: Rotate with a cereal for 2–3 years.
Destroy crop residue after harvest.
Grow resistant or tolerant varieties.
Reduce plant density slightly in humid regions.
organic: Neem cake soil application reduces soil-borne inoculum.
Pseudomonas fluorescens spray reduces disease severity.
Bordeaux mixture 1% is a low-cost protective spray.
chemical: Chlorothalonil 2 g/L or mancozeb 2 g/L at the first spots.
Hexaconazole 2 ml/L or propiconazole 1 ml/L for a curative effect.
Spray every 12–14 days, up to 3–4 sprays in a wet season.

prevention: Treat seed with Trichoderma or a fungicide before sowing.
Rotate crops and remove volunteer groundnut plants.

name: Groundnut Stem Rot
overview: A soil-borne disease that rots the stem base, causing sudden wilting and death. White cottony fungal growth and mustard-seed-like sclerotia are visible at the collar.
image_cues: Photograph the base of a wilted plant at soil level. Look for white cottony mycelium and small round tan sclerotia.
symptoms: Sudden wilting of the plant with leaves still green, later turning brown
White cottony mycelium at the stem base
Small round tan to brown sclerotia (like mustard seeds) on the stem and soil
Dry rotting of the collar region and pods
favourable: High soil moisture with temperature 25–35 °C
Continuous groundnut cropping and heavy residue
Acidic sandy soils
spread: Sclerotia survive in soil for years. Spread by soil movement, water and infected residue.

cultural: Deep summer ploughing to bury sclerotia.
Rotate with a cereal crop.
Avoid dense planting and excessive irrigation.
Remove affected plants with the surrounding soil.
organic: Trichoderma viride seed treatment and soil application at 5 kg/ha with FYM.
Neem cake application reduces the pathogen population.
Soil solarisation before planting.
chemical: Seed treatment with carbendazim + thiram.
Drench the collar with hexaconazole 2 ml/L or carbendazim 1 g/L.
Apply at the first sign of wilting — later drenches rarely help.

prevention: Trichoderma plus neem cake at sowing gives strong, low-cost protection.
Follow a cereal rotation to reduce soil inoculum.

name: Groundnut Bud Necrosis Virus
pathogen: Groundnut bud necrosis virus (Tospovirus), transmitted by thrips
overview: A thrips-transmitted virus that kills young plants and causes severe stunting, necrosis of the growing point and no pod formation.
image_cues: Photograph the whole plant top. Look for necrosis of the terminal bud, ring spots on leaves and stunted bushy growth.
symptoms: Necrosis of the terminal bud and growing point
Chlorotic ring spots and mottling on leaves
Stunted, bushy plants with small leaves
Death of the plant in early infection; few or no pods in late infection
favourable: High thrips populations in warm dry weather followed by rain
Presence of weed hosts around the field
Continuous groundnut cropping
spread: Spread only by thrips. Virus reservoirs include weeds and other crop hosts.

cultural: Grow tolerant varieties.
Rogue out infected plants early.
Remove weeds that host thrips around the field.
Sow at the recommended time with a uniform plant stand.
organic: Blue sticky traps to monitor and trap thrips.
Neem oil spray reduces thrips activity.
Encourage natural predators such as predatory mites.
chemical: Imidacloprid 0.3 ml/L or fipronil seed treatment for thrips.
Spray acephate or spinosad at the early seedling stage.
Vector control in the first 4–6 weeks is the most critical.

prevention: Treat seed with imidacloprid to control thrips in the vulnerable seedling stage.
Remove infected plants and weed hosts promptly.

name: Soybean Yellow Mosaic Virus
pathogen: Mungbean yellow mosaic virus (Begomovirus), transmitted by whitefly
overview: A whitefly-transmitted virus that produces bright yellow mosaic patches on leaves, stunts plants and can cause total pod loss.
image_cues: Photograph a leaf with clear bright yellow and green mosaic patches. Symptoms are most obvious on the newer leaves.
symptoms: Bright yellow and green mosaic patches on leaves
Yellowing spreads until the whole leaf is yellow
Stunted plants with very few pods
Leaves may become small and puckered
favourable: High whitefly populations in warm dry weather
Continuous soybean cropping
Weed hosts near the field
spread: Transmitted by whitefly; the virus is not spread by seed or contact.

cultural: Grow resistant varieties where available.
Remove infected plants early.
Control weeds that host whitefly.
Avoid late planting that coincides with peak whitefly.
organic: Yellow sticky traps to reduce whitefly numbers.
Neem oil or neem seed kernel extract spray.
Conserve predators such as ladybirds and spiders.
chemical: Seed treatment with imidacloprid or thiamethoxam.
Spray triazophos 1.5 ml/L or imidacloprid 0.3 ml/L for the vector.
There is no cure for the virus — manage whitefly.

prevention: Sow disease-tolerant varieties and treat seed against whitefly.
Rogue out infected plants within the first month.

name: Soybean Rust
overview: A fast-moving rust that can defoliate a soybean crop within 2–3 weeks, causing 30–80% yield loss if it appears before pod filling.
image_cues: Photograph the underside of a leaf. Look for tiny raised reddish-brown pustules scattered over the surface.
symptoms: Tiny reddish-brown pustules mainly on the leaf underside
Angular yellow to brown patches on the upper surface
Rapid yellowing and defoliation starting from the lower canopy
Pods remain small and poorly filled
favourable: Extended leaf wetness with temperature 15–28 °C
High humidity and frequent rain or dew
Dense canopy with poor air movement
spread: Airborne spores travel long distances and spread rapidly within a field.

cultural: Grow resistant or tolerant varieties.
Sow early to escape the late-season epidemic.
Reduce plant density for better air movement.
organic: Sulphur sprays have limited effect.
Neem formulations reduce spore germination modestly.

Azoxystrobin plus a triazole for a strong, long-lasting effect.
Spray with a high volume and good under-leaf coverage.

Use tolerant varieties and destroy volunteer soybean plants.

name: Soybean Aerial Blight (Rhizoctonia)
overview: A soil-borne fungus that attacks the stem base and lower canopy in wet conditions, causing blight and lodging.
image_cues: Photograph the stem base and lower leaves. Look for brown water-soaked lesions with a distinct reddish-brown border.
symptoms: Water-soaked to brown lesions on the stem base and lower leaves
Lesions with a reddish-brown margin
Blighting and collapse of the lower canopy
Webby mycelium visible in prolonged wet weather
favourable: Prolonged wet soil and high humidity
Temperature 25–32 °C
Continuous soybean cropping and heavy residue

Improve drainage in low-lying spots.
Avoid very dense plant populations.
organic: Trichoderma seed treatment and soil application.
Increase soil organic matter to boost antagonistic microbes.
chemical: Seed treatment with carbendazim + thiram.
Hexaconazole 2 ml/L spray directed at the stem base.

prevention: Treat seed with Trichoderma before sowing.
Rotate crops and manage residue.

name: Chickpea Fusarium Wilt
overview: The most important chickpea disease, causing sudden wilting from the seedling stage to podding. Once soil is infested it remains so for years.

Dark brown to black rotting of the root and collar region

Continuous chickpea cropping
Sandy or light soils and low soil organic matter

Rotate with a cereal for at least 3 years.
Deep summer ploughing and soil solarisation.
Avoid excess irrigation and ensure good drainage.

Neem cake soil application reduces pathogen populations.
Use clean, healthy seed.

Rotate out of pulses for 2–3 years.

name: Ascochyta Blight (Chickpea)
overview: A devastating cool-humid disease of chickpea that produces dark lesions on leaves, stems and pods, and can wipe out a crop in a wet winter.

Dark elongated lesions on stems and branches causing them to break
Pod lesions with circular dark spots and shrivelled seeds
Blighting and collapse of the whole plant in severe infections

Prolonged leaf wetness from rain or dew
Dense crop canopy

Rotate with a cereal crop.
Bury or remove crop residue.
Avoid dense planting in high-risk areas.

Bordeaux mixture 1% spray is a low-cost protective option.

Spray protectively when cool, humid weather is forecast.

name: Chickpea Collar Rot
overview: A seedling and collar-region rot that kills young plants in patches, especially in warm moist soil with poor-quality seed.

symptoms: Dark, dry rotting at the collar and root region
Seedlings collapse and die in patches
Black powdery spore mass visible on the affected tissue
Yellowing of older leaves before death

High soil organic residue and poor-quality seed
Damage to seed during sowing

cultural: Use good quality, undamaged seed.
Sow on ridges in soils with a history of collar rot.
Avoid heavy irrigation right after sowing.
organic: Trichoderma seed treatment at 5 g/kg seed.
Neem cake soil application decreases the pathogen population.
chemical: Seed treatment with carbendazim or thiram at 2 g/kg.
Drench affected patches with carbendazim 1 g/L.

Use only well-graded, healthy seed.

name: Alternaria Blight (Mustard)
overview: The most damaging disease of rapeseed-mustard in India. Concentric-ring leaf spots plus dark pod lesions reduce seed filling and oil content.
image_cues: Photograph leaves and pods. Look for round brown spots with concentric rings and a yellow halo; pod lesions are dark and sunken.
symptoms: Round to oval brown spots with concentric rings and a yellow halo
Lesions may merge, causing defoliation in severe cases
Dark sunken lesions on pods and stems
Shrivelled seed with reduced oil content
favourable: Temperature 18–25 °C with high humidity and frequent rain or dew
Dense crop canopy with prolonged leaf wetness
Continuous mustard cropping

cultural: Use certified treated seed of tolerant varieties.
Rotate with a non-host crop.
Produce seed in dry areas to reduce seed inoculum.
Avoid very dense sowing.
organic: Trichoderma seed treatment.
Neem oil or garlic extract sprays give partial control.
Bordeaux mixture 1% applied protectively.
chemical: Seed treatment with mancozeb (4 g/kg) or thiram.
Mancozeb 2.5 g/L or iprodione spray at 45 and 60 days.

Spray protectively if humid weather arrives at flowering.

name: White Rust (Mustard)
overview: Produces white blister-like pustules on the underside of leaves and deforms the inflorescence into a 'stag head' with no seed.
image_cues: Photograph the leaf underside. Look for raised white shiny blisters; also photograph the distorted inflorescence if present.

Yellow patches on the corresponding upper surface
Deformed inflorescence forming a swollen stag head
Reduced flowering and no seed set in stag-head branches
favourable: Cool, humid weather 10–20 °C with dew
Wet condition at the seedling and flowering stages
Continuous mustard cropping

cultural: Use resistant varieties.
Remove and destroy stag-head branches and infected leaves.
Rotate with a non-host crop.
organic: Bordeaux mixture 1% protective spray.
Trichoderma soil and seed application.
chemical: Metalaxyl + mancozeb at 2 g/L spray.
Seed treatment with metalaxyl at 6 g/kg seed.

prevention: Sow resistant varieties and treat seed before sowing.
Remove stag head branches before they release spores.

name: Sclerotinia Stem Rot (Mustard)
overview: A wet-weather disease that rots stems at or near the soil line. White cottony mould with hard black sclerotia is the signature.
image_cues: Photograph the lower stem. Look for bleached stem lesions with white cottony mycelium and hard black irregular sclerotia.

White cottony mycelium on the stem surface
Hard black irregular sclerotia on and inside the stem
Sudden wilting and collapse of the plant
favourable: Cool, wet weather 15–20 °C with high humidity
Dense canopy and poor air movement
Soil kept wet for long periods

cultural: Deep summer ploughing to bury sclerotia.
Rotate with a cereal crop for 3–4 years.
Reduce density and avoid excess irrigation.
Remove and destroy affected plants.
organic: Trichoderma soil application.
Soil solarisation during summer to reduce sclerotia.
chemical: Carbendazim 2 g/L spray on the stem base at the first symptoms.
Iprodione spray is also effective.

Bury sclerotia with deep ploughing.

name: Tomato Early Blight
overview: A common foliar disease of tomato and potato that starts on older lower leaves and works upward. It reduces fruit size and exposes fruit to sunscald.
image_cues: Photograph an older lower leaf. Look for brown spots with concentric rings forming a target-board pattern, surrounded by a yellow halo.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern)
A yellow halo around each spot
Disease starts on older lower leaves and moves upward
Stem lesions and fruit rot near the calyx end
favourable: Warm temperature 24–29 °C with alternating wet and dry periods
High humidity and frequent dew
Nutrient-stressed or weak plants
spread: Soil-borne and residue-borne; spores spread by wind, rain splash and tools.

Mulch to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves.
Rotate away from tomato, potato and brinjal for 2–3 years.
Keep plants well nourished — stress increases susceptibility.
organic: Trichoderma and Bacillus-based bio-fungicides.
Copper-based sprays (Bordeaux mixture 1%) provide protection.
Neem oil reduces spread when used early.
chemical: Mancozeb 2.5 g/L or chlorothalonil 2 g/L every 10–12 days.
Azoxystrobin or difenoconazole 1 ml/L for a curative effect.

Rotate away from solanaceous crops.

name: Late Blight
overview: The most explosive disease of tomato and potato. It can destroy an entire field in a week during cool, wet weather. It also causes the historic Irish potato famine.
image_cues: Photograph the leaf edge and stem. Look for large irregular water-soaked grey-green patches with a white fuzzy mould on the underside in humid conditions.
symptoms: Irregular water-soaked grey-green patches on leaves, often at the tip or edge
White fuzzy mould (sporulation) on the underside of lesions in humid weather
Dark brown to black lesions on stems and petioles
Firm brown rot of tomato fruit and potato tubers at the field surface

Prolonged leaf wetness over 10 hours
Dense canopy with poor ventilation

Increase spacing and improve air movement.
Avoid overhead irrigation in the evening.
Harvest potato tubers only after the haulm is fully dead to avoid tuber infection.

Bio-fungicides give limited control in high pressure.
Grow resistant varieties.

Use certified seed tubers free of the pathogen.

name: Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (Begomovirus), transmitted by whitefly
overview: A whitefly-vectored virus that curls leaves upward, stunts plants and stops fruit production. It is the most damaging virus of tomato in tropical regions.

Yellowing of leaf margins and interveinal areas

Continuous tomato cropping
Weed hosts near the field

Neem oil spray for whitefly suppression.
Encourage parasitoids such as Encarsia.

Spray diafenthiuron or spiromesifen for whitefly, rotating modes of action.

Rogue out infected plants as soon as symptoms appear.

name: Bacterial Wilt
overview: A soil-borne bacterial disease that causes sudden wilting of the whole plant while leaves stay green. Once a field is infested it is very hard to grow solanaceous crops there.

symptoms: Sudden wilting of the whole plant with green leaves
Brown discolouration of the vascular tissue in the stem
Milky white bacterial ooze streaming from a cut stem in water
Rapid collapse and death of the plant

Waterlogged or poorly drained soil
Continuous cropping of tomato, brinjal or chilli

Raise and maintain soil pH around 7.0 with lime.
Improve drainage and avoid waterlogging.
Remove and destroy wilted plants with the surrounding soil.

Trichoderma and Pseudomonas soil application.
Soil solarisation before planting.

Rotate away from solanaceous crops and disinfect tools.

name: Potato Common Scab
overview: A soil-borne bacterium that produces rough, corky lesions on the tuber surface. It does not reduce yield much but badly lowers market quality.
image_cues: Photograph the tuber surface. Look for raised or pitted corky brown lesions in a rough patch.
symptoms: Rough, raised or pitted corky brown lesions on the tuber skin
Lesions do not extend deep into the flesh
Tubers look scabby and are rejected by the market

Dry soil conditions during tuber formation
Continuous potato cropping and fresh manure application

Use certified disease-free seed tubers.
Rotate with a cereal or a legume.
Keep soil moist during tuber formation.

Green manuring with mustard reduces scab incidence.
chemical: Seed treatment with mancozeb at 3 g/L dip.

Rotate out of potato for 3 years.

name: Potato Black Scurf
overview: Black, hard sclerotia stick to the tuber surface like specks of soil that will not wash off. The fungus also causes stem canker and poor emergence.

Stem canker causing reddish-brown lesions at the stem base

Continuous potato cropping with infected seed
Heavy residue in no-till situations

Rotate with a cereal crop.
Harvest promptly in dry weather and avoid skinning.
organic: Seed treatment with Trichoderma viride.
Green manuring to encourage microbial antagonism.
chemical: Seed tuber treatment with boric acid 3% or mancozeb 3 g/L for 20 minutes.
Pencycuron or flutolanil seed treatment where available.

Rotate crops and use clean seed.

name: Onion Purple Blotch
overview: The most important foliar disease of onion. Purple blotches on leaves reduce bulb size, and the disease spreads fast in warm humid weather.

Dense canopy and prolonged leaf wetness
Continuous onion cropping

Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day.
Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Ensure good spacing for air movement.

Bacillus subtilis biospray.
Neem oil spray as a supportive measure.

Difenoconazole 1 ml/L or propiconazole 1 ml/L for a stronger effect.

Spray protectively when warm humid weather is predicted.

name: Onion Downy Mildew
overview: A cool, humid-weather disease that produces pale elongated patches with a grey-violet fuzzy growth on the leaf. It spreads very fast in wet weather.

Prolonged leaf wetness and fog
Dense planting in low-lying fields

Improve air movement and avoid evening irrigation.
Remove volunteer onions around the field.

name: Onion Neck Rot
overview: A storage disease that softens the neck and shoulders of the bulb. Symptoms often appear after harvest during storage, causing major post-harvest losses.

Late nitrogen application

name: Chilli Anthracnose (Fruit Rot)

name: Chilli Powdery Mildew

Dense canopy with poor air movement

name: Chilli Leaf Curl Virus
pathogen: Chilli leaf curl virus (Begomovirus), transmitted by whitefly and thrips

Remove infected plants early.
Control weeds that host the vectors.

organic: Yellow and blue sticky traps to control vectors.
Neem oil spray reduces vector populations.

name: Banana Panama Wilt (TR4)
pathogen: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Tropical Race 4)

Warm soils with poor drainage
Continuous banana cropping with susceptible varieties

name: Banana Sigatoka Leaf Spot
overview: Leaf spotting that kills functional leaf area, reducing bunch weight significantly. Black Sigatoka is the more aggressive form.

Continuous banana cropping

Maintain correct spacing and good drainage.
Grow tolerant varieties and keep the plantation well nourished with potassium.
Bag bunches to protect them.
organic: Mineral oil or neem oil sprays reduce the disease.
Regular deleafing reduces inoculum strongly.
Potassium-rich nutrition improves tolerance.

Continuous banana cropping

Uproot and destroy infected plants including the corm (do not just cut the top).

name: Brinjal Little Leaf

cultural: Uproot and destroy affected plants immediately.
Remove weeds that host the phytoplasma and leafhoppers.
Rotate with a non-host crop.
Use tolerant varieties.
organic: Rogueing out affected plants is the main measure.
Neem oil spray to reduce leafhopper numbers.
Use yellow sticky traps for monitoring.
chemical: Control leafhoppers with imidacloprid or thiamethoxam sprays.
Tetracycline injections give temporary remission but are not practical.

prevention: Rogue out affected plants and manage leafhopper vectors early.
Keep the field and its borders weed-free.

name: Powdery Mildew (General)
overview: A very common white powdery fungal growth on many vegetable crops. It spreads quickly in warm dry days with cool humid nights and can defoliate plants.
image_cues: Photograph the leaf surface where the white powder is thickest. Take a close-up so the powdery texture is visible.
symptoms: White to grey powdery patches on leaves, stems and sometimes fruit
The powder rubs off and leaves yellow or brown tissue underneath
Leaves curl, dry and drop prematurely
Reduced fruit size, sunscald and yield loss
favourable: Warm dry days with cool humid nights and heavy dew
Dense canopy with poor air circulation
Excess nitrogen and shaded, humid conditions
spread: Airborne spores spread long distances in wind. Survives on crop residue and weed hosts.

cultural: Improve air movement and avoid very dense planting.
Avoid excess nitrogen; maintain balanced nutrition.
Remove and destroy infected leaves early.
organic: Wettable sulphur 2 g/L spray.
Potassium bicarbonate (5 g/L) or diluted milk spray (1:9).
Neem oil spray as a supportive treatment.
chemical: Wettable sulphur 2 g/L or dinocap 1 ml/L.
Hexaconazole 2 ml/L or penconazole 0.5 ml/L.
Cover both leaf surfaces for effective control.

prevention: Maintain good airflow and balanced fertilisation.
Sulphur sprays are a cheap and effective preventive.
